objects: GWAS effect estimates; null SNPs; PRS
assumptions: SNP effects estimated with uncertainty; not every SNP affects the trait
conclusion: Unadjusted estimates from all SNPs can produce imprecise scores, motivating effect shrinkage or selection by association thresholds.
scope: Motivation for PRS construction, including threshold selection; no new C+T method is claimed.
span: Given that SNP effects are estimated with uncertainty and since not all SNPs influence the trait under study, the use of unadjusted effect size estimates of all SNPs could generate poorly estimated PRS with high standard error. To address this, two broad shrinkage strategies have been adopted: i) shrinkage of the effect estimates of all SNPs via standard or tailored statistical techniques, and ii) use of P-value selection thresholds as inclusion criteria for SNPs into the score.

objects: Individual PRS; genotypes; GWAS effect estimates
assumptions: Genome-wide summary-statistic GWAS weights; possible scaling or shrinkage
conclusion: A polygenic score estimates individual phenotypic propensity by summing genotypes weighted by corresponding GWAS effect estimates.
scope: Score definition; a conditional phenotype likelihood is not specified.
span: We define polygenic risk scores, or polygenic scores, as a single value estimate of an individual’s propensity to a phenotype, calculated as a sum of their genome-wide genotypes weighted by corresponding genotype effect sizes – potentially scaled or shrunk – from summary statistic GWAS data.

objects: Base GWAS summary statistics; target genotypes and phenotypes
assumptions: PRS analysis with base and target samples
conclusion: PRS analyses require base genome-wide genotype-phenotype summary statistics and target individual genotypes and phenotypes.
scope: Input definition for PRS construction and evaluation.
span: Therefore, PRS analyses can be characterized by the two input data sets that they require: i) base (GWAS) data: summary statistics (e.g. betas, P-values) of genotype-phenotype associations at genetic variants (hereafter SNPs) genome-wide, and ii) target data: genotypes and phenotype(s) in individuals of the target sample.

objects: GWAS P-value cutoff; retained and excluded SNP weights
conclusion: Thresholding sets excluded SNP weights to zero and leaves included GWAS effect estimates unshrunk.
scope: Hard selection rule, not a specified Bayesian prior or an explicit penalized likelihood.
span: (ii) In the P-value selection threshold approach, only those SNPs with a GWAS association P-value below a certain threshold (eg. P < 1×10−5) are included in the calculation of the PRS, while all other SNPs are excluded. This approach effectively shrinks all excluded SNPs to an effect size estimate of zero and performs no shrinkage on the effect size estimates of those SNPs included.

objects: Grid of P-value thresholds; target-trait association
assumptions: The prediction-optimal threshold is unknown beforehand
conclusion: Compute scores over multiple P-value thresholds, test each against the target trait, and optimize prediction.
scope: Optimization over the examined threshold grid; predictive assessment requires protection against overfitting.
span: Since the optimal P-value threshold is unknown a priori, PRS are calculated over a range of thresholds, association with the target trait tested for each, and the prediction optimised accordingly (see Section 4.4).

objects: P-value-ordered forward selection; blocks of SNPs
assumptions: P-value threshold selection with increments between tested thresholds
conclusion: Threshold-based scoring can be viewed as forward selection in GWAS P-value order with block updates determined by threshold increments.
scope: A stated analogy, not equivalence to globally optimal subset selection.
span: An alternative way to view this approach is as a parsimonious variable selection method, effectively performing forward selection ordered by GWAS P-value, involving block-updates of variables (SNPs), with size dependent on the increment between P-value thresholds.

objects: Clumped SNPs; additive genetic effects; marginal GWAS summary statistics
assumptions: Approximation to the PRS from a fully conditional GWAS
conclusion: Summing effects after clumping relies on retained SNPs being largely independent and their effects additive.
scope: C+T approximation to conditional-GWAS scoring; independence is approximate rather than established by a threshold.
span: There are two main options for approximating the PRS that would have been generated from full conditional GWAS: (i) SNPs are clumped so that the retained SNPs are largely independent of each other and thus their effects can be summed, assuming additivity, all SNPs are included and the linkage disequilibrium (LD) between them is accounted for.

objects: Clumping; LD pruning; independent regional effects
assumptions: LD clumping for the standard score
conclusion: Unlike random LD thinning, clumping preferentially selects trait-associated SNPs and can retain multiple independent effects within a region.
scope: Author description of clumping relative to pruning.
span: The reason why the standard approach, though simple, appears to perform comparably to more sophisticated approaches [19,38] may be due to the clumping process capturing conditionally independent effects well; note that, (i) clumping does not merely thin SNPs by LD at random (like pruning) but preferentially selects SNPs most associated with the trait under study, (ii) clumping can retain multiple independent effects in the same genomic region if they exist (it does not simply retain only the most associated SNP in a region).

assumptions: Clumping with a researcher-selected correlation threshold
conclusion: The correlation cutoff used to remove SNPs in LD is typically arbitrary and remains a target for methodological development.
scope: Stated limitation of the standard clumping approach.
span: A criticism of clumping, however, is that researchers typically select an arbitrarily chosen correlation threshold [35] for the removal of SNPs in LD, and so while no strategy is without arbitrary features, this may be an area for future development of the classical approach.

assumptions: PRS association evaluated in target data
conclusion: Overlap between base and target samples must be eliminated because it can substantially inflate target-trait association.
scope: Independence requirement for association interpretation; direct and special-case indirect remedies are described in context.
span: Sample overlap between the base and target data can result in substantial inflation of the association between the PRS and trait tested in the target data [35] and so must be eliminated either, (1) directly: either removing overlapping samples from the target data, or if this removes most/all target individuals, then in the base data followed by recalculation of the base GWAS, or (2) indirectly: if, and only if, the overlapping samples correspond to the entire target sample, and the GWAS that contributed to the base data is available for use, then the overlap can be eliminated using the analytic solution described in [36].

objects: Base-target allele-frequency differences; environmental risk-factor differences; null SNPs
assumptions: Allele frequencies and environmental risk-factor distributions differ between base and target
conclusion: Correlated base-target differences in allele frequencies and environmental risks can generate spurious score associations even after perfect population-structure control in the base GWAS.
scope: Population transfer and stratification limitation for PRS, including C+T.
span: If allele frequencies differ systematically between the base and target data, which may derive from genetic drift or the ascertainment of genotyped variants [44], and if the distributions of environmental risk factors for the trait also differ between the two – both highly likely in most PRS studies – then there is a danger that an association between the PRS and target trait can be generated by differences at null SNPs. Confounding is potentially reintroduced even if the GWAS had controlled for population structure perfectly, because this does not account for correlated differences in allele frequencies and risk factors between the base and target data.
location: choi2018 | bioRxiv v1 (2018-09-14) | 3.4 Population structure and global heterogeneity

assumptions: PRS parameters have been trained on target data
conclusion: Separate base and target data do not by themselves provide out-of-sample evaluation when tuning uses the target; final evaluation needs data independent of training.
scope: Separation of tuning and predictive performance assessment.
span: In the PRS setting involving a base and target data, it would be a misconception to believe that out-of-sample prediction has already been performed because polygenic scoring involves two different data sets, when in fact the training is performed on the target data set, meaning that a third data set is required for out-of-sample prediction. In the absence of an independent data set, the target sample can be subdivided into training and validation data sets, and this process can be repeated with different partitions of the sample, e.g. performing 10-fold cross-validation [56,66,67], to obtain more robust model estimates. However, a true out-of-sample, and thus not overfit, assessment of performance can only be achieved via final testing on a sample entirely separate from data used in training.
location: choi2018 | bioRxiv v1 (2018-09-14) | 4.4 Overfitting in PRS association testing

objects: Permutation empirical P-values; optimized PRS; type I error
assumptions: Association testing rather than individual prediction; no validation data or underpowered cross-validation
conclusion: The authors state that permutation empirical P-values can support testing associations with optimized scores while maintaining appropriate type I error despite score overfitting.
scope: Qualitative author-stated claim; this guide provides no theorem or detailed permutation validity conditions.
span: Without validation data or when the size of the target data makes cross-validation underpowered, an alternative is to generate empirical P-values corresponding to the optimised PRS prediction of the target trait, via permutation [12]. While the PRS itself may be overfit, if the objective of the PRS study is association testing of a hypothesis – e.g. H0: schizophrenia and rheumatoid arthritis have shared genetic aetiology – rather than for prediction per se, then generating empirical P-values offers a powerful way to achieve this while maintaining appropriate type 1 error [12].

objects: Summary-statistic PRS weights; joint individual-level genotype models
conclusion: The guide distinguishes summary-statistic PRS from individual-level-only joint estimation and prediction approaches such as BLUP and LASSO.
scope: Terminological and data-input distinction; no claim of mathematical inequivalence.
span: The use of summary statistic data for the genotype effect size estimates differentiates polygenic scores from phenotypic prediction approaches that exploit individual-level data only, in which genotype effect sizes are typically estimated in joint models of multiple variants and prediction performed simultaneously, such as via best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) [20,21] and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) [22,23].

objects: PRS variance explained; chip heritability; population SNP effects
assumptions: Population-level SNP effects estimated without error in the base GWAS
conclusion: The authors state that error-free population SNP effect estimates would allow target phenotype prediction with variance explained equal to chip heritability.
scope: Idealized PRS statement, not a finite-sample guarantee for tuned C+T; LD and transportability conditions are not formalized here.
span: If the population-level effects of the SNPs were estimated from the GWAS without error, then the PRS could predict the phenotype of individuals in the target data with variance explained equal to the “chip-heritability” (hsnp2) of the trait [25].
